parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman books a regular home cleaning service.
script: Good morning, Sparkle Home Services, Sean speaking.
Hello. I'd like to arrange a regular cleaner for my house.
Certainly. Can I take your name?
Patricia Hale. H, A, L, E.
Fourteen Willow Close. That's W, I, double L, O, W.
How many bedrooms does the house have?
How often would you like the cleaner to come?
I was thinking every two weeks, but with the children, I think every week would be better.
Monday, if possible. The house is always messiest after the weekend.
Our cleaner could arrive at nine a.m. Is that OK?
Perfect. I leave for work at half past eight, though.
Is there anything special you'd like done?
Yes. Could they clean the oven on the first visit? It hasn't been done for ages.
Of course. Do you have any pets? Some of our cleaners have allergies.
We have a cat. She's very friendly.
I'll make sure the cleaner is happy with cats. The cost is sixty pounds per visit.
That's fine. How will the cleaner get in if I'm at work?
Most customers leave a key with us, or with a neighbour.
I'll leave one with my neighbour. She's retired, so she's always at home.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A guide gives information about a cycling tour of a city.
script: Hi everyone, I'm Zoe, and I'll be leading today's cycling tour of the city. Before we set off, a few things.
The tour lasts about three hours, including stops, and we'll cover around fifteen kilometres, mostly on quiet streets and cycle paths.
Most of you have standard bikes, but if anyone would like an electric bike, there are a few available for an extra ten pounds.
Helmets are provided free of charge, and everyone must wear one. That's a company rule.
We keep groups to a maximum of twelve people, so everyone can hear me at each stop.
Here's what we'll see. Our first stop is Canal Street, which is covered in colourful street art by local and international artists.
Then we'll cross the Stone Bridge, the oldest bridge in the city, built in the thirteenth century.
At Market Square, there's a food market, and we'll stop for a coffee and a snack.
After that, there's a short climb up Castle Hill, where you'll get the best view over the whole city.
Poet's Corner is where the city's most famous author lived. Her house is now a small museum.
And we'll finish at the Old Quad, the centre of the university, which was founded more than five hundred years ago.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two biology students, Ruby and Kwasi, plan a field trip.
script: Ruby, let's finalise the plans for our biology field trip.
OK. We've agreed on the coastal nature reserve rather than the woodland, haven't we?
Yes, because we're studying marine life. How are we getting there?
The department is providing a minibus from the university. That's much easier than the train.
Good. And the main activity will be sampling rock pools.
Right. My main concern is safety. We need to check the tide times carefully, because the tide comes in very fast there.
Definitely. And the report is due two weeks after the trip.
Now, equipment. The department will provide the quadrats for measuring areas.
Can you bring the waterproof notebooks? You've got a set already.
Yes, I'll bring them. The department will also give us a first aid kit.
I'll bring the identification guides. I borrowed them from the library.
I'll bring mine. It's waterproof, so it's ideal.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on how animals see colour.
script: Today I'd like to talk about how different animals see colour, and why the world looks very different depending on who is looking.
Humans see colour using cells in the eye called cones. Most of us have three types, sensitive to different wavelengths of light, which allows us to see a wide range of colours.
Dogs, by contrast, have only two types of cone. They are not completely colour-blind, as people often think, but they see a more limited range, mainly blues and yellows.
Bees can't see red, but they can see ultraviolet light, which is invisible to us. Many flowers have ultraviolet patterns, known as nectar guides, which direct bees towards the nectar.

The record for colour receptors may belong to the mantis shrimp, which has up to sixteen types of photoreceptor. Surprisingly, experiments suggest that it is quite poor at telling similar colours apart. It may process colour in a very different, faster way.
Most birds have four types of cone, including one sensitive to ultraviolet. Many birds have ultraviolet patterns on their feathers that we can't see, and they use them when choosing mates.
Some snakes, such as pit vipers, have special organs that detect heat, which allows them to find warm-blooded prey in complete darkness.
Reindeer can see ultraviolet light, which may help them to spot lichen, their main winter food, against the snow.
Finally, cuttlefish appear to be colour-blind, yet they are masters of camouflage, changing colour to match their background. How they do this is still a puzzle.

passages.title: The Mystery of Stonehenge
paragraphs: Stonehenge, on Salisbury Plain in southern England, is one of the most famous prehistoric monuments in the world. It was not built all at once. Construction began around 3000 BC with a circular ditch and bank, and the stones were added and rearranged in several stages over the following 1,500 years.

The monument contains two main types of stone. The huge sarsens, some weighing over 25 tonnes, are a type of sandstone. In 2020, chemical analysis showed that most of them came from West Woods, about 25 kilometres to the north. The smaller bluestones are more mysterious. Geologists have traced them to the Preseli Hills in west Wales, around 225 kilometres away. Although a few researchers have argued that glaciers carried them most of the way, most archaeologists believe that people transported them, perhaps on wooden sledges.

In 2024, another surprise emerged. The large flat stone at the centre of the monument, known as the Altar Stone, was found to have come not from Wales, as had long been assumed, but from north-east Scotland, more than 700 kilometres away. How it was moved such a distance remains unknown.

The purpose of Stonehenge has been debated for centuries. The monument is aligned with the sunrise at the summer solstice and the sunset at the winter solstice, suggesting that it was connected with the movements of the sun and the changing seasons. It was also used as a burial site: the cremated remains of many people have been found there. Some researchers have suggested that the bluestones were believed to have healing powers.

Clues to the people who built it have come from Durrington Walls, a large settlement about three kilometres away. Excavations there uncovered the remains of houses and huge quantities of animal bones, especially from pigs, many of which appear to have been killed in midwinter. Archaeologists believe that the settlement housed the workers who built Stonehenge and hosted great feasts.

Stonehenge was declared a World Heritage Site in 1986, and today it attracts more than a million visitors a year. For decades there has been controversy over a busy road that runs close to the monument. A plan to replace it with a tunnel was strongly opposed by archaeologists, who feared damage to the surrounding landscape, and it was cancelled by the government in 2024.

passages.title: The World Inside Us
paragraphs: The human body is home to trillions of microorganisms, most of them living in the gut. For many years, it was often said that bacterial cells in the body outnumbered human cells by ten to one. A more careful estimate published in 2016 concluded that the numbers are roughly equal. Even so, the community of microbes in our intestines, known as the gut microbiome, is now recognised as playing a major role in health.

Gut bacteria perform many useful jobs. They break down dietary fibre that our own digestive system cannot digest, producing substances that nourish the cells lining the intestine. Some also produce vitamins, including vitamin K, and help to train the immune system to distinguish between harmful and harmless organisms.

The variety of species in the gut differs greatly between populations. Studies of the Hadza, a group of hunter-gatherers in Tanzania who eat a diet rich in fibre from wild plants, have found that their gut microbiomes are far more diverse than those of people in industrialised countries. Researchers believe that Western diets, high in processed food and low in fibre, have reduced the diversity of our microbes.

Antibiotics, while life-saving, can also disrupt the microbiome by killing beneficial bacteria along with harmful ones. In some patients, this allows a dangerous bacterium called Clostridioides difficile to take hold, causing severe diarrhoea. A treatment known as faecal microbiota transplantation, in which gut bacteria from a healthy donor are transferred to the patient, has proved remarkably effective, curing around 90 percent of patients with recurring infections.

Some of the most intriguing research concerns the connection between the gut and the brain. Experiments on germ-free mice, which are raised in sterile conditions without any microbes, have found that they respond differently to stress than normal mice. Such studies suggest that gut bacteria may influence mood and behaviour, although it is not yet clear how far these findings apply to humans.

Interest in the microbiome has created a booming market for probiotic supplements and drinks, which contain live bacteria. However, the evidence for their benefits in healthy people is mixed, and many products contain species that do not survive long in the gut. Most scientists agree that the best way to support a healthy microbiome is to eat a varied diet containing plenty of fibre from vegetables, fruit, beans and whole grains.

passages.title: Do We Need Economic Growth?
paragraphs: For most of the past century, governments have treated economic growth, usually measured as an increase in gross domestic product, or GDP, as one of their most important goals. Yet GDP was never intended to measure a nation's wellbeing. When the economist Simon Kuznets helped to develop it in the 1930s, during the Great Depression, his purpose was to measure economic output. He himself warned that the welfare of a nation could hardly be inferred from a measure of national income.

There is no doubt that growth has brought enormous benefits. As economies in Asia and elsewhere have grown, hundreds of millions of people have escaped extreme poverty. According to the World Bank, the share of the world's population living in extreme poverty fell from more than a third in 1990 to less than a tenth by 2019. Growth has also paid for improvements in health, education and infrastructure.

The problem is that growth has historically gone hand in hand with rising consumption of resources and rising greenhouse gas emissions. Some argue that this link can be broken, a process known as decoupling. There is evidence that it is possible: the United Kingdom, for example, has almost halved its emissions since 1990 while its economy has continued to grow. Critics reply that such reductions are far too slow to prevent dangerous climate change, and that they partly reflect the movement of manufacturing to other countries.

These concerns have given rise to the 'degrowth' movement, whose supporters argue that wealthy countries should deliberately reduce their production and consumption, focusing instead on reducing working hours, improving public services and sharing resources more equally.

Others propose measuring progress differently. Bhutan has long used an index of Gross National Happiness alongside GDP, and in 2019 New Zealand introduced a 'wellbeing budget', in which government spending was guided by measures of mental health, child poverty and the environment as well as economic output.

In my view, the debate is often framed too simply. For low-income countries, growth remains essential to reduce poverty, and it would be unjust to ask them to give it up. For wealthy countries, I believe degrowth is politically unrealistic, since few voters would accept a deliberate fall in living standards. A more promising path is for rich countries to focus on wellbeing rather than GDP alone, while investing heavily in green technologies that allow economies to prosper within the limits of the planet.

task1.text: The line graph below shows unemployment rates in four countries between 2008 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The line graph compares unemployment rates in Spain, the USA, Germany and Japan between 2008 and 2024.

Overall, Spain had by far the highest unemployment rate throughout the period, with dramatic fluctuations, while Japan consistently had the lowest. Germany's rate fell steadily, and the USA's rose and fell twice.

In 2008, Spain's unemployment rate was 11%, compared with 7.5% in Germany, 5.8% in the USA and 4% in Japan. Over the next four years, unemployment in Spain more than doubled to a peak of 25%, and the US rate also increased, to 8.1%. In contrast, Germany's rate fell to 5.4%, and Japan's rose only slightly.

After 2012, Spain's unemployment declined gradually, reaching 11.5% in 2024, close to its original level. The US rate fell to 4.9% in 2016, rose again to 8.1% in 2020, and then dropped to 4%. Meanwhile, the rates in Germany and Japan continued to fall steadily, ending the period at 3.4% and 2.5% respectively.

task2.text: Some people think that all schools should teach children how to cook. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Write at least 250 words.
model: As ready meals and fast food have become more common, fewer young people learn to cook at home. This has led some people to argue that cooking should be taught in all schools. I strongly agree with this view, because cooking is an essential life skill with benefits for health, independence and even academic learning.

The most important reason is health. Many diet-related illnesses, such as obesity and type 2 diabetes, are linked to a reliance on processed food that is high in sugar, salt and fat. Children who learn to prepare simple, healthy meals are more likely to eat well as adults. Cooking lessons can also teach them to understand food labels and plan balanced meals on a limited budget, which is particularly valuable for families with low incomes.

Cooking also prepares young people for independent life. Many students leave home for university or work without being able to make even a basic meal, and they often spend too much money on takeaways. Moreover, cooking can support other subjects: measuring ingredients involves mathematics, and understanding how food changes when it is heated involves science.

Some people argue that cooking should be taught by parents, and that schools should focus on academic subjects in an already crowded timetable. However, not all parents have the time, skills or resources to teach their children, and leaving it to families means that the children who most need these skills are least likely to learn them.
In conclusion, I believe that cooking should be a compulsory part of the school curriculum, because it improves health, prepares children for adult life and reinforces other learning.

speaking.cue:
Describe a family member you admire.
You should say:
- who this person is
- what they do
- what they are like
and explain why you admire them.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about my mother, who I admire more than anyone else I know. She's a primary school teacher, and she's been teaching in the same government school for almost twenty-five years. What I admire most is her patience and her energy. She teaches classes of more than forty children, many of them from very poor families, and she still comes home talking about individual students: one who has finally learned to read, or another who needs extra help because his father is ill. On top of her job, she has looked after our whole family, including my grandmother, who lived with us for many years. She's also one of the most curious people I know. A few years ago, she decided to learn how to use a computer properly, so she could create more interesting lessons, and now she makes her own slides and videos for her class. I think I admire her because she shows that you don't need a famous job to make a real difference to people's lives. She has also taught me that it's never too late to learn something new, which is something I try to remember whenever I find my studies difficult.
